_readme: Questions with known answers, used by eval/run.py to measure retrieval.
EVERY expected uid was checked against state.db before being written here:
the paper exists, is not retired, survives scoring.is_junk, and is therefore
in the 9,032-paper index. A golden set naming papers retrieval cannot reach
measures nothing, and run.py prints a warning if that ever becomes true.
'why' records what in the paper actually answers the question. It is there so
a later reader can audit a question rather than trust it -- a golden set is
only as good as its labels, and unaudited labels rot silently.
TIERS
abstract  the answer is in the abstract, in roughly the paper's own words.
Should pass today; a fall here is a regression.
vocab     the answer is in the abstract but the question is asked the way a
practitioner would ask it, avoiding the paper's vocabulary. Tests
whether the embedding generalises past surface word overlap.
fulltext  the answer is ONLY in the body -- a sample definition, a data
source, a section the abstract never mentions. These are EXPECTED
TO FAIL now: retrieval reads abstracts and nothing else. That
failure is the measurement of the gap docs/ft/ is meant to close.
Multi-paper answers are deliberate. recall@k asks what share of them arrive,
hit@k asks whether any did; a question whose evidence is spread over two
papers is the normal case in this archive, not an edge case.

questions.q: Is the profitability of the currency carry trade compensation for risk, or something else?
questions.why: Abstract reviews three explanations for carry and momentum profitability, the first being compensation for bearing risk.

questions.q: How do currency carry trade returns change as the maturity of the foreign bond increases?
questions.why: Abstract: returns to carry trades decrease as the maturity of the foreign bonds increases, with local term premia offsetting currency risk premia.

questions.q: Does equity time-series momentum keep working at valuation extremes?
questions.why: Abstract: momentum performs well in mid-valuation regimes but breaks down near historical valuation extremes.

questions.q: Is the optimal factor timing portfolio the same thing as the stochastic discount factor?
questions.why: Abstract opens by stating the optimal factor timing portfolio is equivalent to the SDF.

questions.q: Can deep neural networks with economic restrictions improve multifactor timing?
questions.why: Abstract: economically motivated restrictions, multitask learning plus LSTM, outperforming benchmarks.

questions.q: How are graph neural networks being applied to asset and investment management?
questions.why: The first is an explicit practitioner overview of GNNs in asset management; the second tests whether adding graph structure improves financial forecasting.

questions.q: Do crowded trades explain the returns to well-known equity anomalies?
questions.why: Abstract: anomaly risk-adjusted returns are primarily generated by the most/least crowded stocks in each leg.

questions.q: Does volatility management or factor mean-variance optimisation beat equal weighting out of sample?
questions.why: Abstract compares recursive factor mean-variance, volatility-managed factors and 1/N over nine equity factors, 1976-2025.

questions.q: What is the limiting distribution of a volatility target index as the rebalancing step goes to zero?
questions.why: Abstract states two limit theorems and derives the exact limiting distribution as the rebalancing time step approaches zero.

questions.q: Does volatility scaling improve a multi-asset portfolio relative to a static 60/40 benchmark?
questions.why: Abstract compares four strategies including a static 60/40 benchmark across equities, fixed income, inflation-linked and commodities.

questions.q: Can machine learning time the currency carry and dollar factors?
questions.why: Abstract: whether ML can improve the timing of the two fundamental currency factors, carry and dollar, using 264 predictors.

questions.q: Can hidden Markov models with heavy-tailed emissions reproduce the stylised facts of daily equity returns?
questions.why: Abstract: whether an HMM generator reproduces heavy tails, negligible linear autocorrelation and slow decay of absolute-return autocorrelation.

questions.q: Why have fast systematic signals stopped paying since the financial crisis?
questions.why: The paper is a microstructural account of short-term trend ceasing to deliver since roughly 2009. The question avoids 'trend following' entirely.

questions.q: When two of my core signals disagree with each other, what does the evidence say a macro book should do?
questions.why: Draws lessons on trend following versus carry from bonds, gold and 2022. Question names neither signal.

questions.q: How do practitioners keep realised portfolio risk roughly constant through time?
questions.why: Both concern targeting a fixed risk level by dynamically adjusting exposure; the question says neither 'volatility scaling' nor 'target'.

questions.q: Does holding the same positions as everyone else cost you return?
questions.why: Crowded trades and anomaly returns, asked without the word 'crowded'.

questions.q: Can you tell in advance which style premium is worth leaning on?
questions.why: Both are factor timing papers; the question uses the desk phrase 'style premium' rather than 'factor'.

questions.q: What makes a price-continuation signal break down when markets are unusually expensive or unusually cheap?
questions.why: Momentum breaking down at valuation extremes, asked without the word 'momentum'.

questions.q: Does filtering entries on an implied volatility index improve a managed futures programme?
questions.why: A VIX-adjusted trend model revisited out of sample. 'Implied volatility index' and 'managed futures' are the practitioner terms for VIX and trend following.

questions.q: Can the relationships between companies be used to improve return forecasts?
questions.why: Both are graph-structure-for-forecasting papers; the question never says graph, network or neural.

questions.q: How much of a diversified futures book's return comes from tactical tilts rather than the static allocation?
questions.why: Abstract: timing-based tilts across asset classes drive much of the risk and return of a diversified cross-asset portfolio.

questions.q: Is a naive equal allocation hard to beat once you account for estimation error?
questions.why: The 1/N versus optimisation comparison, asked in the classic 'estimation error' framing the abstract does not use.

questions.q: Which study fits its regime model to ten years of daily SPY prices and holds out everything from January 2024 onward for out-of-sample testing?
questions.why: Body, 'Data and model': SPY from 2014-01-03 to 2024-01-03 in sample (2,516 days), 2024-01-04 to 2026-04-20 out of sample. The abstract names neither SPY nor any date.

questions.q: Which paper predicts the dominant principal components of anomaly returns using book-to-market ratios?
questions.why: Body sections 'Dominant Components of the Factors', 'Predicting the Large PCs of Anomaly Returns' and Table 2 on BE/ME. The abstract mentions none of this.

questions.q: Which currency study sorts portfolios by their forward discount and reports the betas of currency-based risk factors?
questions.why: Body sections 'Portfolios of currencies sorted by their forward discount' and 'Betas of currency-based factors'. The abstract says only carry and momentum.

questions.q: Which cross-asset futures study uses Barchart end-of-day data on sixteen of the most liquid CME contracts?
questions.why: Body, section II DATA: Barchart end-of-day continuous contracts, sixteen liquid CME futures. The abstract names no data vendor.

questions.q: Which carry trade study builds signals from relative Nelson-Siegel yield curve factors?
questions.why: Body section 'Relative Nelson-Siegel Yield Factors'. The abstract lists carry, value, momentum and the forward curve, never Nelson-Siegel.

questions.q: Which paper uses a G-10 panel of nine developed bond markets with the United States as the domestic country?
questions.why: Body, 'Data': Australia, Canada, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, UK, against the US. The abstract gives no sample.

questions.q: Which commodity study introduces a projection method to turn contract-level predictions into calendar spread trades?
questions.why: Body, 'Proposed Method': defines the CS strategy, proves efficacy, and introduces a projection method. The abstract describes only the hierarchical graph representation.

questions.q: Which portfolio choice paper validates its theory against an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driver state with an affine conditional mean?
questions.why: Body, 'Experiments': controlled tests against an OU driver state and affine conditional mean. The abstract states the geometric setup only.
